projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Sheldon Stover was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Okay, my name is Technical Sergeant Deanna Fox, and it is 8 October, Friday afternoon, at 12:45. I'm sitting here at the Desert Storm Enlisted Club on Luke Air Force Base with Chief Master Sergeant Retired Smokey Stover. He currently lives at 2062 Peoria, Arizona. Okay, the first question I'm going to ask you, sir, is were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: You enlisted, okay. Now, where were you living at the time you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: In Berrien Center, Michigan.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: So why did you join the military?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Because everybody after Pearl Harbor -- and I was the right age to enlist, rather than be drafted. And I could have been exempt because I was living on a farm, but I chose to enlist in the Air Force in lieu of being drafted.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Okay, I just wanted to ask about your experiences. Which wars did you actually serve in?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: World War II, Korea, and Vietnam, and over in the Cold War (________+).

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: And where exactly did you go, as far as where you got stationed during those wars?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: I was at China-Burma-India Theater during World War II and Mariana Islands and B-29s. And during the Korean War, I was actually on a B-50 flying mainly out of Europe. Because of being a nuclear carrier, we were rotated in and out of Europe about every 90 days. And during the Vietnam War, I was Bomber Branch Chief in Riverside, California on B-52 (________+) airplanes flying there, and over to Guam and to Thailand.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Oh. Were there any casualties in your unit?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: During World War II, we had numerous casualties, both air and ground. As far as flying was concerned, the B-29 was not a proven airplane, so a lot of times you got shot up, and you would crash or ditch on the way home. And we weren't (________+) jet streams at that time. We would get into high headwind over Japan and couldn't get back home on the amount of gas (________+).

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Sir, were you a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Well, that's good. That's good news. Okay, I'm going to move over to talk about your family life. How did you stay in touch with family while you were gone?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Just by letters, mainly. We didn't have E-mails and stuff then that we have now. Once in a while in the B-47 days when I was a crew chief flying into French Morocco on the airplane, and I'd go to (________+) and talk to my wife through the MARS System they had back in those days.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: What does MARS stand for?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Military -- I don't know. It is military radio intercept.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Okay, that wasn't on here (________+). Do you recall what the food was like -- the food you used to eat (________+)?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: During World War II, in-flight lunches was J-Rations. And during -- an all dried food, basically. Eggs was powdered eggs. Meat was canned meat. If we had anything fresh, it was usually liver because the (________+) stole all the steaks and stuff when they unloaded the ships. The rest was basically regular meals. As far as dry rations were concerned, even out of Europe we had an in-flight kitchen and they fed us.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Did you have three meals a day?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Depends. If you're flying, you usually carry something with you that you can heat in a hot cup, or soup or something, on an extended mission. Some of our B-50 missions during the Cold War was as high as $20.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Okay, did you always have plenty of supplies, that includes medical supplies, as far as equipment to do your job? Did you always have plenty of clothes?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Well, the B-29 program during World War II was a first. It was the only airplane that ever went to combat that did not have a test program. And we took it into war right off the assembly line, and we had numerous problems that we had to have down time to correct. Our maintenance people were sent by boat, and they never made it to India before we left India, and China, going to Mariana Islands. And because -- by the time they got to the Mariana Islands, the war was over. So we really didn't have maintenance people, per se (________+). We done our own maintenance.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: I'm actually looking forward to asking you this next question. Was there something special you did for good luck? Some people carry a rabbit's foot, or?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Not that I know of. There was a lot of times I was scared, but just got lucky. I don't know why. I didn't have a good luck charm.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: All right. So how did people entertain themselves?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Well, mainly we listened to Tokyo Rose to see if she had any news about us during World War II. The rest of the time was just spent while I was -- I was a good pinochle player. I was a good domino player. When I was on a flight crew, any time that you're sitting around waiting to fly, we done that. We had no TV. So, it was just a different lifestyle than it is today.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: All right. Do you recall any particular humorous or unusual events?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Well, during World War II, we had all of our pilots nicknamed. Like a guy that rode the (brigs) on the airplane, he was taxying, we called him Speedy. And we called another guy Roaring Joe. We all had our names. We had a guy by the name of (________+). Every time he went on a mission, he encountered flack. And every time -- and his answer was -- if the question was: Did you encounter flack? And he'd say: Naturally. And did you get hit? Naturally. Did you have somebody wounded on your crew? Naturally. And so we called him Naturally (________+). And it was closeness amongst the crews. Because in India and China, we had a lot of malaria and dysentery, so you didn't always fly with the same crew. In fact, very seldom did you have a whole crew, per se. We always had to get one or more people. And so some people -- and I was one of them that would fly that was most (________+) had no choice. Sometimes going to another squadron, which I never did. As long as I stayed within the squadron, I replaced about any crew that they ever asked me to replace.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: What were some of the pranks that you and others would actually pull?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Oh, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: You won't get in trouble for this one.

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Well, most of the -- most of the things that we did were something like put a sign on somebody like, Kick Me, or something that he didn't know about. Because most of us, especially during World War II, when we was flying and doing maintenance at the same time, we didn't have too much time for pranks of any kind. But after that, it was mostly, Kick me, and things like this. Because when you're around aircraft, you have so many safety features that you are not bumping into people, or pinching somebody, or something like that, because they are liable to jump in front of a propeller or jet engine or something.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Okay, did you ever keep a personal diary?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: You did not? Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Where were you?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Forth Worth, Texas. I was in headquarters (SAK) Engineering Division. Because of the F-111 program general dynamics, we had been there for three years.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Okay, what did you do in the days and weeks afterward?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Went fishing.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Went fishing. Did you ever work or go back to school?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Yes, I worked. I was in a copy machine business. I sold plumbing supplies for a while. Then I was in the copy machine business for about ten years. We had leased and maintained copy machines, but mainly in the grocery stores, (________+) Winn-Dixie. I had Dallas area for five years, and then I had the Fort Worth area for five years.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Was your education supported by the G.I. Bill?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: I did not take any additional training after the war. I was an airplane mechanic. I left a specialist armor, gunnery system engineer, and I had been in school in all of that. And other than military schools, like the NCO Academy, which I went to and graduated in class 56G, (________+) after the second (________+). I went to F-111 Program General Dynamics. I was in there for three years. And that was a requirement to make Senior Chief. You had to be an academy graduate, so I jumped on that before the Senior Chiefs came out.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships in the service?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Hundreds.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Did you continue any of those friendships?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: For how long?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Forever.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Until they die off.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: So your --

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: There is -- I'm one of the few left.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Did you join any veteran organizations?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Yes. I'm a member of the DAV, lifetime member. And lifetime member of the Noncommissioned Officers Association. And I'm a lifetime member of a couple of the other associations.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Do you ever attend a reunion?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Every year.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Every year faithfully?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Faithfully. I go to three different ones from my World War II outfit, second bombing, and the B-52, which was the 33rd bombing. And one of them is every year. My World War II is out there -- the second bombing, this year was the last year. We were down to like 37 people. And then the 58th bombing was every two years -- 58 bombing -- 58, (________+) there was only two (________+) 43rd and three -- there's only two wings, 43rd and 305th, and we all know each other. (________+).

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: How did your service experience affect your life?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Oh, I'm sure it made me a better person. Get up in the morning and go to bed at night. I still had the farm in that position, because I go to bed with the chickens and I get up with them.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: I'm looking at a letter certificate you received from the Maricopa County Sheriff's office. If you could please just give us a quick synopsis of how you earned this certificate?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Well, we had a -- this is after the actual (________+) Years ago, a gentleman come in and shot up our homeowners association. He had enough ammunition to have killed all of us that was attending the meeting. He had four weapons, and he was firing them. And one guy -- you have probably seen in the Readers Digest, and some of the other stories about the man that actually tackled him and knocked him off his feet is a heart transplant man. And he was going out the door to go to his doctor's appointment when this gentleman pushed him back inside and yelled that he was going to kill everybody. And he immediately started shooting. And he sit down with an AR-15, one of the weapons that he had, and started shooting with a .22 pistol. And after ten rounds with the pistol, he ran out of ammo, and he reached over to get the AR-15. And in that time, Mr.(________+) knocked him off his feet. And even though he was a heart transplant, his wife didn't want him wrestling with anybody, so his wife hollered that he needed help, and we all jumped up and went over to help him. And from that shooting -- he was still shooting during the time when we got the weapon away from him, and he was laying on top of the weapon when the last round went off. He had his hand on the trigger and jammed the weapon because it couldn't eject the shell. And by that time we had him tied up and roped and prevented him from getting two more weapons that he had in a huge front pocket with rounds in the chamber and in the clip. Both -- of both weapons. He had actually 600 rounds of ammo. And from that I received this award from the Sheriff, along with the city of Peoria, and DAV's award and VFW's award for saving (________+) lives. He actually killed two people and wounded three more.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: That's definitely (________+). The last question I have for you -- actually it is not a question. Is there anything that you would like to add that we have not covered in this interview?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: I don't know. I have so many different stories happened to me, and my wife dying. That I was in the first refueling of KB-29s and B-50s. We used a 300-foot hose -- before they had booms. I went to (________+) fumes, and from there was refueling aircraft. And was an instructor in that for a while. That's a dangerous job, and it is not a good system to use here, although the British had been using it since 1932. Another thing during the B-47s, we used to refuel KC-97, the aircraft, and we (________+) the airplane flying, trying to deliver fuel to a jet. It has to slow down to pick up fuel, and as you get a heavy weight, you can get high on the B-47 and get into the (________+) of the tank, and it will flip you. I got flipped upside down. As crew chief, I was -- rode what they called the idiot seat in the B-47. A small ejectable seat. And went upside down about 5000 foot. Later we recovered the aircraft, both highs, lows, (________+). We went to altitude to save fuel, and we were going to land in the Azores and went to the city of (Somine,) and we had too high crosswinds and had to go to the city of (Somine.) And flying at 42,000, we got up there (________+) low speed and high speed is almost unrecognizable for a pilot at that point. They made a straight-in approach from 42,000 (________+) and couldn't -- to the city of (Somine,) and couldn't taxi up then on fuel was all but one engine. And that's about the scariest thing that ever happened.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: I thought of one more question on my own. My curiosity. Where did you pick up your name, Smokey?

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: In 1940 there was a funny paper named Smokey Joe. It was written by Al Capp, I believe. But my initials are S. J. And when I went into military service in '42, nobody asked me my name. I was known as Smokey Joe, and I went by it every since.

sp.speaker: Deanna Fox
sp.p: Well, sir, that about does it. I want to thank you for sharing that recollection. Let me repeat that, your recollection, and taking the time out to participate in the Veterans History Project.

sp.speaker: Sheldon Stover
sp.p: Okay, I appreciate it. ( End of interview.)
